title: Give me your hand (Berakhot 5b)
hookLine: Rabbi Yochanan heals others, but when ill needs a friend: a prisoner can't free himself
last: NOT EVERY PAIN IS A LESSON.

cards: A man who spent a whole career handing other people what they needed now can't get up off his own couch, and he won't let anyone help. The Talmud has a man like that.
Rabbi Yochanan visits the sick sage, hears neither they nor their reward, and says it plainly: give me your hand. The sage gives it, and Rabbi Yochanan raises him up.
Then, a few lines later, Rabbi Yochanan falls ill himself.

teach.b: Rabbi Chanina comes to visit him, and asks the very question Rabbi Yochanan had asked: are your sufferings dear to you? Neither they nor their reward. Give me your hand.
He gives it, and Rabbi Chanina raises him. Now the Talmud stops and asks the obvious thing. Rabbi Yochanan could raise others.
Why couldn't he raise himself? The answer is one line: a prisoner cannot free himself from prison. That's the whole lesson, and it isn't about weakness.
The healer's power was real; he had just used it on someone else. But the hand that lifts you has to come from outside your own cell.
Pain has walls, and from inside them you can't reach the latch. There's a quiet humility in who ends up helped. The one with the healing hand is the one on the bed, saying yes to someone else's.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in this story the healer can raise others but not himself, and the Talmud doesn't call that a flaw. It calls it being a prisoner. The fix isn't trying harder.
Give me your hand is the ask, and holding it out is the answer.

how: Many synagogues say a prayer for healing, the Mi Sheberach, naming people who are ill, and visiting the sick, bikur cholim, is counted a mitzvah in Jewish tradition.

games.q: what does “give me your hand” mean?
o: a request to be lifted by someone outside your pain
a promise sealed by shaking hands over a deal
a blessing given by laying hands on a child

games.q: who lifts whom — tap the pairs.

s: in the story, Rabbi Yochanan heals himself when he falls ill
Rabbi Chanina visits and raises him: a prisoner can't free himself.
the Talmud asks outright why the healer couldn't raise himself
and answers in one line: a prisoner cannot free himself from prison.
needing help is shown in this story as a flaw in the healer
the Talmud calls it being a prisoner; the hand has to come from outside.

games.q: your coach, who helps everyone, sprains her ankle before a tournament and insists she's fine on her own. what does Berakhot 5b point to?
o: offer your hand anyway; nobody frees themselves from their own prison.
trust her; someone who helps others knows best how to help herself.
say nothing; offering help to a helper would only embarrass her.
games.why: Rabbi Yochanan raised others and still needed Rabbi Chanina's hand. the Talmud doesn't fault him; it just says the hand comes from outside.

practice: Think of one thing you've been carrying alone this week: a heavy bag, a form, a worry. Picture the person who'd help if you asked, and rest one open hand, palm up, on your knee as if you were holding it out to them.
Stay like that for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Give me your hand. Rabbi Yochanan's words to the sick, and then Rabbi Chanina's to him: a prisoner can't free himself.

orig.note: Aramaic: give me your hand, said at each sickbed on Berakhot 5b.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: give me your hand, and let someone else do the lifting. Berakhot, day five.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 5b (Rabbi Yochanan raises Rabbi Chiya bar Abba; Rabbi Yochanan falls ill and Rabbi Chanina raises him; 'a prisoner cannot free himself from prison')
